claim: Corruption is commonly defined as 'the abuse of entrusted power for private gains'
source: Corruption, commonly defined as 'the abuse of entrusted power for private gains' (Graycar and Smith, 2011), is one of the most pervasive and complex social problems today.
evidence: The definition is attributed to a citation (Graycar and Smith, 2011)

claim: Corruption distorts development priorities
source: It distorts development priorities, aggravates inequality in societies, and challenges organizations and governments globally (Mauro, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mauro, 1995

claim: Corruption aggravates inequality in societies
source: It distorts development priorities, aggravates inequality in societies, and challenges organizations and governments globally (Mauro, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mauro, 1995

claim: Corruption challenges organizations and governments globally
source: It distorts development priorities, aggravates inequality in societies, and challenges organizations and governments globally (Mauro, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mauro, 1995

claim: Bribery costs between 1500 and 2000 billion US dollars each year (~2% of the global GDP)
source: One of the most common forms of corruption is bribery, which costs between 1500 and 2000 billion US dollars each year (~2% of the global GDP) (Gaspar and Hagan, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gaspar and Hagan, 2016

claim: Bribery usually occurs in an interpersonal context in which at least two parties are involved, a briber and a power-holder
source: It usually occurs in an interpersonal context in which at least two parties are involved, a briber and a power-holder.
evidence: Supported by citations to Abbink, 2006 and Köbis et al., 2016 in the following sentence

claim: In bribery, the briber often pays the power-holder in some way, and, in return, the power-holder makes decisions that profit the briber
source: The briber often pays the power-holder in some way, and, in return, the power-holder makes decisions that profit the briber (Abbink, 2006; Köbis et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abbink, 2006 and Köbis et al., 2016

claim: A bribe takes place when the briber obtains a favorable treatment or an advantageous outcome by paying the power-holder to circumvent a norm of impartiality or a moral rule
source: That is, a bribe takes place when the briber obtains a favorable treatment or an advantageous outcome by paying the power-holder to circumvent a norm of impartiality or a moral rule (Köbis et al., 2016; Serra and Wantchekon, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Köbis et al., 2016 and Serra and Wantchekon, 2012

claim: Bribery often implies harming the interests of a third party, which can be an explicit person or a societal organization
source: In addition, bribery often implies harming the interests of a third party, which can be an explicit person or a societal organization (Barr and Serra, 2009; Köbis et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barr and Serra, 2009 and Köbis et al., 2016

claim: Two forms of moral costs are incurred by the power-holder who takes a bribe: conniving with a fraud committed by the briber and harming an innocent third party
source: Thus, one can distinguish two forms of moral costs incurred by the power-holder who takes a bribe: conniving with a fraud committed by the briber and harming an innocent third party.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the preceding discussion of bribery characteristics

claim: People are reluctant to tell a self-serving lie or inflict physical harm on an anonymous partner for their own benefit even when there is no material cost of doing so
source: For example, people are reluctant to tell a self-serving lie or inflict physical harm on an anonymous partner for their own benefit even when there is no material cost of doing so (Crockett et al., 2017; Rosenbaum et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crockett et al., 2017 and Rosenbaum et al., 2014

claim: The ventral part of anterior insula (vAI) has been shown to be engaged when moral and social norms are violated
source: On the one hand, the ventral part of anterior insula (vAI) has been shown to be engaged when moral and social norms are violated.
evidence: Supported by citations in the following sentences

claim: A stronger vAI signal has been observed when people are deceived by another person
source: For instance, a stronger vAI signal has been observed when people are deceived by another person (Yin and Weber, 2016) or when deciding whether to lie to obtain additional gains (Yin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yin and Weber, 2016

claim: A stronger vAI signal has been observed when deciding whether to lie to obtain additional gains
source: For instance, a stronger vAI signal has been observed when people are deceived by another person (Yin and Weber, 2016) or when deciding whether to lie to obtain additional gains (Yin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yin et al., 2017

claim: The temporoparietal junction (TPJ) has been found to contribute to balance personal interests and other's welfare
source: On the other hand, the temporoparietal junction (TPJ) has been found to contribute to balance personal interests and other's welfare (Hutcherson et al., 2015; Morishima et al., 2012; Obeso et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hutcherson et al., 2015; Morishima et al., 2012; Obeso et al., 2018

claim: TPJ is more active when one's decision impacts a person who is in a disadvantageous situation
source: This region is also more active when one's decision impacts a person who is in a disadvantageous situation.
evidence: Supported by citations in the following sentences

claim: Multivoxel patterns of TPJ can discriminate generous from selfish choices during charitable decision-making
source: For instance, a recent fMRI study found that multivoxel patterns of TPJ can discriminate generous from selfish choices during charitable decision-making (i.e., donating to help someone else in desperate need) (Tusche et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tusche et al., 2016

claim: The posterior part of TPJ encoded the levels of other's need when individuals decided whether to help another person
source: Another study showed that the posterior part of TPJ encoded the levels of other's need when individuals decided whether to help another person (Hu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2017

claim: The ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) is known to be the hub of value computation for both non-social and social decisions
source: Since the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) is known to be the hub of value computation for both non-social (Bartra et al., 2013) and social decisions (Ruff and Fehr, 2014), we predicted the recruitment of vmPFC in computing an integrative decision value signal preceding the decision of whether to accept a bribe.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bartra et al., 2013 and Ruff and Fehr, 2014

claim: The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is key to support the pursuit of moral goals in a context-dependent manner
source: A recent theory argues that the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is key to support the pursuit of moral goals in a context-dependent manner (Carlson and Crockett, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carlson and Crockett, 2018

claim: The dlPFC plays a critical role in causally modulating self-serving dishonest behaviors
source: In particular, the dlPFC plays a critical role in causally modulating self-serving dishonest behaviors (Maréchal et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2014) and norm-enforcing decisions (Buckholtz et al., 2015; Knoch et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maréchal et al., 2017 and Zhu et al., 2014

claim: The dlPFC plays a critical role in causally modulating norm-enforcing decisions
source: In particular, the dlPFC plays a critical role in causally modulating self-serving dishonest behaviors (Maréchal et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2014) and norm-enforcing decisions (Buckholtz et al., 2015; Knoch et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Buckholtz et al., 2015 and Knoch et al., 2006

claim: A recent fMRI study identified selective recruitment of the dlPFC in evaluating ill-gotten money obtained by harming others (vs. self)
source: A recent fMRI study also identified selective recruitment of the dlPFC in evaluating ill-gotten money obtained by harming others (vs. self) (Crockett et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Crockett et al., 2017

claim: Recent work has highlighted the modulatory role of dlPFC on the value signal in vmPFC especially when the decision-making process requires individuals to exert self-control to inhibit the impulse to choose immediate rewards (vs. long-term rewards)
source: More intriguingly, recent work has highlighted the modulatory role of dlPFC on the value signal in vmPFC especially when the decision-making process requires individuals to exert self-control to inhibit the impulse to choose immediate rewards (vs. long-term rewards; Hare et al., 2009; Hare et al., 2014) or personal profits (vs. moral values; Baumgartner et al., 2011; Dogan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hare et al., 2009 and Hare et al., 2014

claim: Recent work has highlighted the modulatory role of dlPFC on the value signal in vmPFC especially when the decision-making process requires individuals to exert self-control to inhibit the impulse to choose personal profits (vs. moral values)
source: More intriguingly, recent work has highlighted the modulatory role of dlPFC on the value signal in vmPFC especially when the decision-making process requires individuals to exert self-control to inhibit the impulse to choose immediate rewards (vs. long-term rewards; Hare et al., 2009; Hare et al., 2014) or personal profits (vs. moral values; Baumgartner et al., 2011; Dogan et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baumgartner et al., 2011 and Dogan et al., 2016

claim: The dlPFC signal is linked to individual variations in the levels of self-serving dishonesty
source: A growing body of literature links the dlPFC signal to individual variations in the levels of self-serving dishonesty (Dogan et al., 2016; Yin and Weber, 2018) or harm aversion (Crockett et al., 2017), which are closely related with two types of moral costs specific to corrupt acts measured in the current task.
evidence: Supported by citations to Dogan et al., 2016 and Yin and Weber, 2018

claim: The dlPFC signal is linked to individual variations in harm aversion
source: A growing body of literature links the dlPFC signal to individual variations in the levels of self-serving dishonesty (Dogan et al., 2016; Yin and Weber, 2018) or harm aversion (Crockett et al., 2017), which are closely related with two types of moral costs specific to corrupt acts measured in the current task.
evidence: Supported by citation to Crockett et al., 2017

claim: Participants were less likely to accept an offer in the Dyad scenario
source: Mixed-effect logistic analyses showed that participants were less likely to accept an offer in the Dyad scenario (main effect of the scenario: χ2(1)=8.53, p=0.003) and in the Bribe condition (main effect of the proposer's conduct: χ2(1)=25.3, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data

claim: Participants were less likely to accept an offer in the Bribe condition
source: Mixed-effect logistic analyses showed that participants were less likely to accept an offer in the Dyad scenario (main effect of the scenario: χ2(1)=8.53, p=0.003) and in the Bribe condition (main effect of the proposer's conduct: χ2(1)=25.3, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data

claim: A significant two-way interaction was observed with respect to whether the offer was accepted (χ2(1)=4.73, p=0.030)
source: More importantly, we observed a significant two-way interaction with respect to whether the offer was accepted (χ2(1)=4.73, p=0.030; see Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data and referenced in Figure 2A

claim: Participants were much less likely to accept bribes (vs. offers in the Control condition) in the Dyad scenario, where a third party was involved (acceptance rate: 61.6 ± 22.6% vs. 82.8 ± 13.2%; odds ratio = 0.15, b = −1.91 [–2.83, –1.25], SE = 0.41, p<0.001)
source: Simple-effect analyses further revealed that participants were much less likely to accept bribes (vs. offers in the Control condition), in the Dyad scenario, where a third party was involved (acceptance rate: 61.6 ± 22.6% vs. 82.8 ± 13.2%; odds ratio = 0.15, b = −1.91 [–2.83, –1.25], SE = 0.41, p<0.001), in comparison to the Solo scenario (acceptance rate: 67.0 ± 20.7% vs. 83.3 ± 14.8%; odds ratio = 0.13, b = −2.03 [–2.77, –1.08], SE = 0.39, p<0.001; see Supplementary file 1a for details of the regression output).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data

claim: Participants were much less likely to accept bribes (vs. offers in the Control condition) in the Solo scenario (acceptance rate: 67.0 ± 20.7% vs. 83.3 ± 14.8%; odds ratio = 0.13, b = −2.03 [–2.77, –1.08], SE = 0.39, p<0.001)
source: Simple-effect analyses further revealed that participants were much less likely to accept bribes (vs. offers in the Control condition), in the Dyad scenario, where a third party was involved (acceptance rate: 61.6 ± 22.6% vs. 82.8 ± 13.2%; odds ratio = 0.15, b = −1.91 [–2.83, –1.25], SE = 0.41, p<0.001), in comparison to the Solo scenario (acceptance rate: 67.0 ± 20.7% vs. 83.3 ± 14.8%; odds ratio = 0.13, b = −2.03 [–2.77, –1.08], SE = 0.39, p<0.001; see Supplementary file 1a for details of the regression output).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data

claim: Model 5 was identified as the winning model based on hierarchical Bayesian model comparison
source: Based on hierarchical Bayesian model comparison (see Supplementary file 1b), we identified Model 5 (Equation 1) as the winning model
evidence: Supported by model comparison results from the study data

claim: Parameter recovery analysis showed that true estimates positively correlated with the recovered estimates for all parameters across individuals involved in the winning model (Pearson correlation: rs > 0.71, ps <0.001)
source: Parameter recovery analysis showed that these true estimates (i.e., values we obtained from the actual choice data that we collected) positively correlated with the recovered estimates (i.e., what we obtained from the simulated data generated with these true parameters) for all parameters across individuals involved in the winning model (Pearson correlation: rs > 0.71, ps <0.001; see Figure 2—figure supplement 2; see Materials and methods for details)
evidence: Supported by parameter recovery analysis results from the study data

claim: The posterior predictive check revealed that the proportion of acceptance predicted by the winning model successfully recovered the actual proportion of acceptance (all conditions: the within-sample PPC: rs > 0.90, ps <0.001; the out-of-sample PPC: rs > 0.68, ps <0.001)
source: The posterior predictive check (PPC) further revealed that the proportion of acceptance predicted by this model successfully recovered the actual proportion of acceptance (all conditions: the within-sample PPC: rs > 0.90, ps <0.001; the out-of-sample PPC: rs > 0.68, ps <0.001; see Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplement 4, and Materials and methods for details)
evidence: Supported by posterior predictive check results from the study data

claim: Participants weighed the payoffs for themselves positively (βPH: 16.02 ± 2.47, t(38) = 40.51, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 6.49)
source: Further analyses of the individual-level posterior mean of these parameters revealed that participants weighed the payoffs for themselves positively (βPH: 16.02 ± 2.47, t(38) = 40.51, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 6.49) but did not do so for the proposer (βP: −0.88 ± 2.48, t(38) = −2.21, p=0.033, Cohen's d = −0.35).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data

claim: Participants did not weigh the payoffs for the proposer positively (βP: −0.88 ± 2.48, t(38) = −2.21, p=0.033, Cohen's d = −0.35)
source: Further analyses of the individual-level posterior mean of these parameters revealed that participants weighed the payoffs for themselves positively (βPH: 16.02 ± 2.47, t(38) = 40.51, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 6.49) but did not do so for the proposer (βP: −0.88 ± 2.48, t(38) = −2.21, p=0.033, Cohen's d = −0.35).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data

claim: Participants decreased the weights of their own payoffs when they were being bribed (θ: 5.94 ± 4.28, t(38) = 8.67, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.39)
source: Moreover, participants decreased the weights of their own payoffs when they were being bribed (θ: 5.94 ± 4.28, t(38) = 8.67, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.39) and apparently displayed concern for the financial loss of the innocent third party (ω: 0.97 ± 0.82, t(38) = 7.32, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.17; see Figure 2B; also see Supplementary file 1c for the bivariate correlation between all parameters in the winning model).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data and shown in Figure 2B

claim: Participants displayed concern for the financial loss of the innocent third party (ω: 0.97 ± 0.82, t(38) = 7.32, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.17)
source: Moreover, participants decreased the weights of their own payoffs when they were being bribed (θ: 5.94 ± 4.28, t(38) = 8.67, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.39) and apparently displayed concern for the financial loss of the innocent third party (ω: 0.97 ± 0.82, t(38) = 7.32, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.17; see Figure 2B; also see Supplementary file 1c for the bivariate correlation between all parameters in the winning model).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data and shown in Figure 2B

claim: Participants disliked the inequality in the absolute payoff between themselves and the proposer (γ: −2.35 ± 2.23, t(38) = −6.59, p<0.001, Cohen's d = −1.06)
source: In addition, participants also disliked the inequality in the absolute payoff between themselves and the proposer (γ: −2.35 ± 2.23, t(38) = −6.59, p<0.001, Cohen's d = −1.06).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data

source: Mixed-effect linear regression on log-transformed RT) showed that participants responded slower in the Dyad scenario (main effect of the scenario: F(1, 5567)=15.52, p<0.001), in the Bribe condition (main effect of the proposer's conduct: F(1, 5570)=64.28, p<0.001), and when they rejected the offer (main effect of decision: F(1, 5582)=50.08, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data

claim: Participants responded slower in the Bribe condition (main effect of the proposer's conduct: F(1, 5570)=64.28, p<0.001)
source: Mixed-effect linear regression on log-transformed RT) showed that participants responded slower in the Dyad scenario (main effect of the scenario: F(1, 5567)=15.52, p<0.001), in the Bribe condition (main effect of the proposer's conduct: F(1, 5570)=64.28, p<0.001), and when they rejected the offer (main effect of decision: F(1, 5582)=50.08, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data

claim: Participants responded slower when they rejected the offer (main effect of decision: F(1, 5582)=50.08, p<0.001)
source: Mixed-effect linear regression on log-transformed RT) showed that participants responded slower in the Dyad scenario (main effect of the scenario: F(1, 5567)=15.52, p<0.001), in the Bribe condition (main effect of the proposer's conduct: F(1, 5570)=64.28, p<0.001), and when they rejected the offer (main effect of decision: F(1, 5582)=50.08, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data

claim: A two-way interaction was detected between the decision (accept/reject) and the proposer's conduct (bribe/control; F(1, 5575)=20.79, p<0.001)
source: Moreover, we detected a two-way interaction between the decision (accept/reject) and the proposer's conduct (bribe/control; F(1, 5575)=20.79, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data

claim: Participants responded more slowly when they accepted offers in the Dyad scenario (vs. Solo; b = 0.07 (0.03, 0.11), SE = 0.02, t(4093) = 3.724, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.12)
source: Post-hoc analyses further showed that participants responded more slowly when they accepted offers in the Dyad scenario (vs. Solo; b = 0.07 (0.03, 0.11), SE = 0.02, t(4093) = 3.724, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.12) or when the proposer was bribing them (vs. Control; b = 0.20 (0.16, 0.24), SE = 0.02, t(4095) = 9.990, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.31).

claim: Participants responded more slowly when the proposer was bribing them (vs. Control; b = 0.20 (0.16, 0.24), SE = 0.02, t(4095) = 9.990, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.31)
source: Post-hoc analyses further showed that participants responded more slowly when they accepted offers in the Dyad scenario (vs. Solo; b = 0.07 (0.03, 0.11), SE = 0.02, t(4093) = 3.724, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.12) or when the proposer was bribing them (vs. Control; b = 0.20 (0.16, 0.24), SE = 0.02, t(4095) = 9.990, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.31).
evidence: Supported by statistical test results from the study data

claim: Stronger engagement of the left vAI was observed in the Bribe (vs. Control) condition regardless of scenarios (peak MNI coordinates: −40/10/−6, t(114) = 3.81, p(SVC-FWE)=0.025) when investigating brain regions encoding the expected personal profits
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, we observed stronger engagement of the left vAI in the Bribe (vs. Control) condition regardless of scenarios (peak MNI coordinates: −40/10/−6, t(114) = 3.81, p(SVC-FWE)=0.025) when investigating brain regions encoding the expected personal profits (i.e., the profits earned by participants had they accepted the offer).
evidence: Supported by fMRI analysis results from the study data

claim: The right vAI delineated similar neural responses (peak MNI coordinates: 36/12/–14, t(114) = 3.27, p(SVC-FWE)=0.090)
source: To examine the lateralization of this effect, we lowered the statistical threshold and found that the right vAI delineated similar neural responses (peak MNI coordinates: 36/12/–14, t(114) = 3.27, p(SVC-FWE)=0.090; see Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by fMRI analysis results from the study data and shown in Figure 3A

claim: The right vAI displayed an increased sensitivity to the expected personal gains in the Dyad (vs. Solo) scenario (peak MNI: 36/14/–14; t(114) = 3.86, p(SVC-FWE)=0.022)
source: We also found that the right vAI displayed an increased sensitivity to the expected personal gains in the Dyad (vs. Solo) scenario (peak MNI: 36/14/–14; t(114) = 3.86, p(SVC-FWE)=0.022), whereas the left vAI showed a similar trend that did not reach statistical significance (peak MNI: −36/10/−16; t(114) = 3.09, p(SVC-FWE)=0.146; see Supplementary file 1f for results of other contrasts under a lenient threshold).
evidence: Supported by fMRI analysis results from the study data

claim: A stronger activity in the dorsal part of anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) was observed during bribery-related decision-making (i.e., event contrast: Bribe vs. Control) across scenarios, under a whole-brain threshold
source: In addition, we also observed a stronger activity in the dorsal part of anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) during bribery-related decision-making (i.e., event contrast: Bribe vs. Control in GLM1c; same below) across scenarios, under a whole-brain threshold (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by fMRI analysis results from the study data and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: A strong involvement of the right TPJ, extending to the posterior part of the superior temporal sulcus (pSTS), was observed in encoding the expected losses incurred by the innocent third party due to bribe-taking (peak MNI coordinates: 54/–-48/–4, t(38) = 4.70, p(SVC-FWE)=0.010)
source: As predicted, we observed a strong involvement of the right TPJ, extending to the posterior part of the superior temporal sulcus, in encoding this PM (pSTS; peak MNI coordinates: 54/–-48/–4, t(38) = 4.70, p(SVC-FWE)=0.010; see Figure 3B; also see Supplementary file 1f for other activated regions).
evidence: Supported by fMRI analysis results from the study data and shown in Figure 3B

claim: The decision-relevant multivoxel activation patterns of TPJ/pSTS only dissociated the bribery-related decision-making in the Dyad (DB vs. DC; two-choice forced-alternative accuracy ± SE: 69.2 ± 11.1%, p=0.024; ppermutation = 0.020) but not the Solo scenario (SB vs. SC; 53.8 ± 8.6%, p=0.749; ppermutation = 0.300)
source: However, using a post-hoc multivariate-based decoding analysis with a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validated approach, we found that the decision-relevant multivoxel activation patterns of TPJ/pSTS only dissociated the bribery-related decision-making in the Dyad (DB vs. DC; two-choice forced-alternative accuracy ± SE: 69.2 ± 11.1%, p=0.024; ppermutation = 0.020) but not the Solo scenario (SB vs. SC; 53.8 ± 8.6%, p=0.749; ppermutation = 0.300; see Figure 3C; also see Figure 3—figure supplement 3 for decoding results of the left and right TPJ/pSTS).
evidence: Supported by multivariate decoding analysis results from the study data and shown in Figure 3C

claim: The vmPFC was more engaged in integrating the value signals in the Bribe condition (peak MNI coordinates: 0/34/–10, t(38) = 4.73, p(SVC-FWE)=0.007)
source: As expected, the vmPFC was more engaged in integrating the value signals in the Bribe condition (peak MNI coordinates: 0/34/–10, t(38) = 4.73, p(SVC-FWE)=0.007).
evidence: Supported by fMRI analysis results from the study data

claim: A smaller effect was also observed in the Control condition (peak MNI coordinates: 0/52/–10, t(38) = 3.76, p(SVC-FWE)=0.064)
source: A smaller effect was also observed in the Control condition (peak MNI coordinates: 0/52/–10, t(38) = 3.76, p(SVC-FWE)=0.064; see Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by fMRI analysis results from the study data and shown in Figure 4A

claim: A supplementary pattern similarity analysis revealed a significantly positive correlation between multivoxel vmPFC patterns of value computation in the Bribe and the Control conditions (r = 0.14 ± 0.36, p(permutation)=0.023)
source: A supplementary pattern similarity analysis revealed a significantly positive correlation between multivoxel vmPFC patterns of value computation in the Bribe and the Control conditions (r = 0.14 ± 0.36, p(permutation)=0.023; see Figure 4B, C).
evidence: Supported by pattern similarity analysis results from the study data and shown in Figure 4B, C

claim: vmPFC, together with bilateral middle/inferior temporal gyri and posterior cingulate cortex extending to cuneus, correlated positively with the relative SV signal
source: We found that vmPFC, together with bilateral middle/inferior temporal gyri and posterior cingulate cortex extending to cuneus, correlated positively with the relative SV signal (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1; also see Supplementary file 1g for other activated regions).
evidence: Supported by fMRI analysis results from the study data and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: An increased anti-corruption signal in the dlPFC was found in the Dyad scenario compared with the Solo scenario (left dlPFC: peak MNI coordinates: −38/48/18, t(96) = 3.70, p(SVC-FWE)=0.024; right dlPFC: peak MNI coordinates: 42/50/16, t(96) = 3.52, p(SVC-FWE)=0.050)
source: We found an increased anti-corruption signal in the dlPFC in the Dyad scenario compared with the Solo scenario (left dlPFC: peak MNI coordinates: −38/48/18, t(96) = 3.70, p(SVC-FWE)=0.024; right dlPFC: peak MNI coordinates: 42/50/16, t(96) = 3.52, p(SVC-FWE)=0.050; see Supplementary file 1h for other activated regions).
evidence: Supported by fMRI analysis results from the study data

claim: Post-hoc analyses revealed that the anti-corruption signal in the dlPFC was significantly higher than 0 only in the Dyad scenario (ps <0.002), but not the Solo scenario (ps >0.056)
source: Importantly, post-hoc analyses revealed that the anti-corruption signal in the dlPFC was significantly higher than 0 only in the Dyad scenario (ps <0.002), but not the Solo scenario (ps >0.056; see Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by post-hoc analysis results from the study data and shown in Figure 5A

claim: A negative correlation was observed between the functional coupling of the vmPFC and the right dlPFC during bribery-related decision-making (i.e., PPI contrast: Bribe vs. Control) and the parameter θ (peak MNI coordinates: 46/36/30, t(37) = 4.78, p(SVC-FWE)=0.005)
source: However, we observed a negative correlation between the functional coupling of the vmPFC and the right dlPFC during bribery-related decision-making (i.e., PPI contrast: Bribe vs. Control) and the parameter θ(peak MNI coordinates: 46/36/30, t(37) = 4.78, p(SVC-FWE)=0.005; see Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by functional connectivity analysis results from the study data and shown in Figure 5B

claim: The control analysis confirmed the results in the right dlPFC after ruling out the effect of parameter ω (peak MNI coordinates: 46/36/30, t(36) = 4.58, p(SVC-FWE)=0.014)
